about: Short notes on landmark Supreme Court of India judgments, written for Samvidhan AI. They summarise what each judgment held in plain words; they are not the judgment text. Read the full judgment before relying on a case. Law-report citations are given only where well established (AIR = All India Reporter, SCC = Supreme Court Cases).

cases.name: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
cases.topics: preventive detention, procedure established by law, due process, personal liberty
cases.held: The Court upheld the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 (except one section). The majority read 'procedure established by law' in Article 21 to mean any procedure laid down by a law made by the legislature, refusing to read in American-style 'due process'. It also treated each fundamental right separately, so a detention law was tested only against Articles 21 and 22, not Article 19.
cases.later: This narrow approach was rejected in R.C. Cooper (1970) and Maneka Gandhi (1978).

cases.name: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras
cases.topics: freedom of the press, ban on a journal, circulation, public order
cases.held: The Madras government banned the entry and circulation of the journal Cross Roads in the State. The Court held that freedom of speech and expression includes the freedom to circulate ideas, and struck the ban down, because Article 19(2) as it then stood did not allow restrictions for 'public order'.
cases.later: Parliament responded with the First Amendment (1951), which added 'public order' and other grounds to Article 19(2).

cases.name: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan
cases.topics: caste-based reservation in college admissions, communal G.O., directive principles
cases.held: Madras reserved seats in medical and engineering colleges by caste and religion (the 'Communal G.O.'). The Court struck it down under Article 29(2), which forbids denying admission to state-funded institutions on grounds of religion, race or caste, and held that the Directive Principles cannot override fundamental rights.
cases.later: The First Amendment (1951) added Article 15(4), so that the State can make special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

cases.name: State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar
cases.topics: equality before law, reasonable classification, arbitrariness, special courts
cases.held: The Court struck down a West Bengal law that let the government send any case it chose to special courts with a shorter procedure. Article 14 allows the State to classify, but a classification must rest on an intelligible difference that has a rational connection to the purpose of the law; unguided power to pick and choose cases is arbitrary.

cases.name: I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab
cases.topics: amendment of fundamental rights, Parliament's amending power, prospective overruling
cases.held: By 6 to 5, the Court held that a constitutional amendment is 'law' under Article 13, so Parliament cannot amend the Constitution to take away or abridge fundamental rights. To avoid unsettling earlier land-reform amendments, it applied the ruling only to future amendments ('prospective overruling').
cases.later: Parliament responded with the 24th Amendment (1971), and Golaknath was overruled in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

cases.name: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
cases.topics: basic structure doctrine, amending power, judicial review, constitutional amendment limits
cases.held: By 7 to 6, the largest bench in the Court's history held that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution under Article 368, including fundamental rights, but cannot damage or destroy its 'basic structure'. Features named as basic include the supremacy of the Constitution, democracy, secularism, the separation of powers and federalism. It overruled Golaknath (1967) and struck down the part of Article 31C that stopped courts from checking whether a law really gives effect to the Directive Principles.
cases.later: The basic structure doctrine has been applied in many later cases, such as Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), Minerva Mills (1980) and the NJAC case (2015).

cases.name: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
cases.topics: election of the Prime Minister, 39th Amendment, free and fair elections, basic structure
cases.held: The 39th Amendment (1975) added Article 329A(4) to put the Prime Minister's election beyond challenge in any court. The Court struck that clause down for violating the basic structure, including free and fair elections and judicial review.
cases.later: Article 329A was later omitted by the 44th Amendment (1978).

cases.name: Additional District Magistrate, Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla
cases.topics: Emergency, habeas corpus, suspension of fundamental rights, detention without trial
cases.held: During the 1975-77 Emergency, a Presidential order under Article 359 suspended the right to move courts to enforce Article 21. By 4 to 1, the Court held that detained persons could not then ask a High Court for habeas corpus, even to argue that their detention was illegal. Justice H.R. Khanna dissented, holding that the Constitution is not the only source of the right to life and liberty.
cases.later: The 44th Amendment (1978) changed Article 359 so that Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended during an Emergency. In K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) the Supreme Court said this judgment was seriously flawed and overruled it.

cases.name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
cases.topics: passport, right to travel abroad, procedure established by law, fair procedure, natural justice
cases.held: The government impounded Maneka Gandhi's passport without giving reasons or a hearing. The Court held that the 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 must be fair, just and reasonable, not arbitrary, and that Articles 14, 19 and 21 must be read together. The right to travel abroad is part of personal liberty. This greatly widened Article 21 and moved away from A.K. Gopalan (1950).

cases.name: Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar
cases.topics: speedy trial, undertrial prisoners, bail, free legal aid, jail
cases.held: A public interest petition showed that thousands of undertrial prisoners in Bihar had spent years in jail, often longer than the maximum sentence for their offence. The Court held that a speedy trial is part of the right to life and liberty under Article 21, ordered the release of many undertrials, and said the State must provide free legal aid to people who cannot afford a lawyer.

cases.name: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab
cases.topics: death penalty, capital punishment, rarest of rare cases, sentencing
cases.held: By 4 to 1, the Court upheld the death penalty for murder as constitutional, but said it may be given only in the 'rarest of rare' cases, when the alternative of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed. Courts must weigh the aggravating and mitigating circumstances of both the crime and the criminal.

cases.name: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India
cases.topics: basic structure, 42nd Amendment, limited amending power, directive principles and fundamental rights
cases.held: The Court struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368, added by the 42nd Amendment, which tried to make Parliament's amending power unlimited and beyond judicial review. It also struck down the change that let laws for any Directive Principle override Articles 14 and 19 under Article 31C. Limited amending power, judicial review and the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are part of the basic structure.

cases.name: Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India
cases.topics: bonded labour, forced labour, public interest litigation, quarry workers
cases.held: A letter about bonded labourers in stone quarries near Delhi was treated as a writ petition. The Court held that bonded labour violates Article 23 and the right to live with dignity under Article 21, ordered the identification, release and rehabilitation of bonded labourers, and confirmed that public interest litigation can be brought on behalf of people who cannot reach the courts themselves.

cases.name: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
cases.topics: right to livelihood, pavement dwellers, slum eviction, shelter, notice before eviction
cases.held: Pavement and slum dwellers in Bombay challenged their eviction. The Court held that the right to life under Article 21 includes the right to livelihood, so a person cannot be deprived of it except by a fair and reasonable procedure, such as notice and a hearing. It did not give a right to occupy public footpaths, and allowed the evictions after the monsoon, with alternative sites for some of the dwellers.

cases.name: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum
cases.topics: maintenance after divorce, Muslim women, section 125 CrPC, uniform civil code
cases.held: The Court held that a divorced Muslim woman who cannot maintain herself can claim maintenance from her former husband under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a law that applies to people of all religions. It also regretted that Article 44 (a uniform civil code) had remained a dead letter.
cases.later: Parliament then passed the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, which the Court read in Danial Latifi (2001) as still requiring a fair and reasonable provision for the divorced wife.

cases.name: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak)
cases.topics: industrial accident, hazardous industry, absolute liability, environment, compensation
cases.held: After oleum gas leaked from a Shriram factory in Delhi in 1985, the Court laid down the rule of 'absolute liability': an enterprise carrying on a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity must compensate everyone harmed by an accident in it, with none of the usual exceptions. The compensation should be large enough to deter, in proportion to the size of the enterprise.

cases.name: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala
cases.topics: national anthem, freedom of religion, freedom of expression, right to remain silent, school students
cases.held: Three children of the Jehovah's Witnesses faith were expelled from school because, for religious reasons, they stood respectfully but did not sing the national anthem. The Court ordered them taken back: no law required singing, and forcing them to sing would violate their freedom of speech and expression (which includes the right to remain silent) and their freedom of religion.

cases.name: Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu
cases.topics: anti-defection law, Tenth Schedule, Speaker's decision on disqualification, judicial review
cases.held: The Court upheld the Tenth Schedule (the anti-defection law). The Speaker or Chairman deciding a disqualification acts as a tribunal, and the decision can be challenged in court on limited grounds, such as mala fides or a violation of natural justice. By majority, paragraph 7, which barred courts altogether, was held invalid because it had not been ratified by half of the States as Article 368(2) requires.

cases.name: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
cases.topics: OBC reservation, Mandal Commission, creamy layer, 50 percent ceiling, reservation in promotions
cases.held: The Court upheld 27% reservation in central government jobs for Other Backward Classes (the Mandal Commission report). It held that the 'creamy layer' among backward classes must be excluded, that reservations should not normally exceed 50%, that there can be no reservation in promotions, and that reservation based only on economic criteria was invalid.
cases.later: Reservation in promotions for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes was later allowed by the 77th Amendment (Article 16(4A)). The 103rd Amendment (2019) introduced up to 10% reservation for economically weaker sections, which was upheld in the EWS reservation case (2022).

cases.name: Unni Krishnan, J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh
cases.topics: right to education, children, free education up to 14, private professional colleges, capitation fees
cases.held: The Court held that every child has a fundamental right to free education until the age of 14, flowing from the right to life in Article 21 read with Article 45. Beyond that age, the right depends on the State's economic capacity. It also framed a scheme for admissions and fees in private professional colleges.
cases.later: The 86th Amendment (2002) added Article 21A, making free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 an express fundamental right. The fee scheme was overruled in T.M.A. Pai Foundation (2002).

cases.name: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
cases.topics: President's Rule, dismissal of a state government, floor test, secularism, federalism
cases.held: The Court held that a proclamation of President's Rule under Article 356 can be reviewed by the courts. Whether a State government has lost its majority must be tested on the floor of the Assembly, not decided by the Governor's opinion, and the Assembly should not be dissolved before Parliament approves the proclamation. Secularism and federalism are part of the basic structure.

cases.name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
cases.topics: arrest guidelines, custodial torture, custodial death, police, arrest memo, rights of arrested persons
cases.held: To stop custodial torture and deaths, the Court laid down requirements for every arrest and detention: police officers must carry clear identification; prepare an arrest memo signed by a witness and the arrested person; inform a friend or relative; tell the person of these rights; have them medically examined; and let them meet a lawyer during interrogation. Breaking these rules can lead to departmental action and contempt of court, and the State must pay compensation for custodial violence.

cases.name: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
cases.topics: sexual harassment at the workplace, women employees, guidelines, gender equality, dignity
cases.held: Filed after the gang rape of a social worker in Rajasthan, this case led the Court to declare that sexual harassment at the workplace violates the rights to equality, to practise any profession, and to life with dignity. As there was no law, it used international conventions such as CEDAW to lay down binding 'Vishaka guidelines', including a complaints committee headed by a woman in every workplace.
cases.later: Parliament replaced the guidelines with the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013.

cases.name: T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka
cases.topics: minority educational institutions, linguistic and religious minorities, private colleges, admissions and fees
cases.held: An 11-judge bench held that whether a group is a religious or linguistic minority under Article 30 is decided State by State. Minorities have the right to establish and administer educational institutions, and every citizen may run a private educational institution as an occupation under Article 19(1)(g), but the State may regulate standards, fees (to prevent profiteering) and fair admissions.

cases.name: Prakash Singh v. Union of India
cases.topics: police reforms, transfers and postings of police officers, police complaints authority, political interference
cases.held: On a petition by a former police chief, the Court ordered the States to reform their police: set up a State Security Commission to keep political pressure off the police; give the Director General of Police and key officers a minimum tenure of two years; create a Police Establishment Board for transfers and postings; separate investigation from law-and-order duties; and set up Police Complaints Authorities to hear complaints of serious misconduct.

cases.name: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu
cases.topics: Ninth Schedule, judicial review, basic structure, protected laws
cases.held: Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule are protected by Article 31B from challenge for violating fundamental rights. The Court held that laws added to the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 (the date of Kesavananda Bharati) can still be struck down if they damage the basic structure, including the rights in Articles 14, 19 and 21.

cases.name: Selvi v. State of Karnataka
cases.topics: narco-analysis, lie detector, polygraph, brain mapping, self-incrimination, police investigation
cases.held: The Court held that forcing an accused, suspect or witness to undergo narco-analysis, a polygraph (lie detector) test or brain-mapping violates the right against self-incrimination in Article 20(3) and personal liberty under Article 21. Such tests may be done only with the person's free consent, and even then the statements made cannot be used as evidence on their own.

cases.name: Lily Thomas v. Union of India
cases.topics: disqualification of MPs and MLAs on conviction, Representation of the People Act, criminal politicians
cases.held: The Court struck down Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, which let sitting MPs and MLAs keep their seats while they appealed against a conviction. Since then, a legislator convicted of an offence and sentenced to two years or more is disqualified from the date of conviction.

cases.name: National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India
cases.topics: transgender rights, third gender, gender identity, self-identification
cases.held: The Court recognised transgender persons as a 'third gender' with the full protection of the fundamental rights, and held that every person has the right to decide their own gender identity. It directed the governments to treat them as socially and educationally backward classes for reservations and to provide welfare schemes, health care and legal recognition.
cases.later: Parliament later passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019.

cases.name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
cases.topics: arrest, police, offences punishable up to seven years, dowry cruelty cases, magistrate, detention
cases.held: The Court held that police must not arrest automatically for offences punishable with imprisonment of up to seven years (such as cruelty to a wife under the former Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code). An officer must first be satisfied that arrest is necessary under the conditions in Section 41 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and record the reasons, and a magistrate must check those reasons before allowing detention.
cases.later: The Code of Criminal Procedure was replaced in 2024 by the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which has similar arrest provisions.

cases.name: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
cases.topics: online speech, Section 66A IT Act, social media posts, offensive messages, internet, chilling effect
cases.held: The Court struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, which made it a crime to send 'grossly offensive' or 'annoying' messages online. Its words were so vague that they caught protected speech and had a chilling effect, and the restriction did not fit any ground in Article 19(2). Discussion and advocacy, however unpopular, are protected; only incitement can be restricted.

cases.name: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India
cases.topics: appointment of judges, National Judicial Appointments Commission, collegium system, judicial independence
cases.held: By 4 to 1, the Court struck down the 99th Amendment and the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, 2014, which had given the government and 'eminent persons' a role in appointing judges. Primacy of the judiciary in appointments is part of judicial independence, a basic feature of the Constitution. The earlier 'collegium' system, in which the senior-most judges recommend appointments, was restored.

cases.name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
cases.topics: right to privacy, data protection, personal autonomy, bodily integrity, personal information
cases.held: A nine-judge bench unanimously held that the right to privacy is a fundamental right, protected mainly by Article 21 and also by the freedoms in Part III. It covers bodily integrity, personal information and personal choices. Any intrusion must be backed by a law, pursue a legitimate aim and be proportionate. The Court overruled earlier cases (M.P. Sharma, 1954 and Kharak Singh, 1962) to the extent they said otherwise.
cases.later: Parliament later passed the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

cases.name: Shayara Bano v. Union of India
cases.topics: triple talaq, instant divorce, Muslim women, talaq-e-biddat
cases.held: By 3 to 2, the Court set aside the practice of instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat), by which a Muslim husband could divorce his wife at once by saying 'talaq' three times.
cases.later: Parliament later made instant triple talaq a criminal offence through the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019.

cases.name: Common Cause v. Union of India
cases.topics: euthanasia, right to die with dignity, living will, advance medical directive, end of life care
cases.held: The Court held that the right to live with dignity under Article 21 includes dying with dignity. It allowed passive euthanasia (withdrawing life support from a terminally ill patient) and recognised 'living wills' (advance medical directives), with safeguards for how they are made and carried out.
cases.later: The Court simplified these safeguards in 2023.

cases.name: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
cases.topics: Section 377, LGBTQ rights, homosexuality, sexual orientation, decriminalisation
cases.held: The Court unanimously held that Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code was unconstitutional to the extent it made consensual sexual acts between adults in private a crime, including between persons of the same sex. Discrimination based on sexual orientation violates equality, dignity, privacy and freedom of expression. It overruled Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013).

cases.name: Joseph Shine v. Union of India
cases.topics: adultery, Section 497 IPC, women's equality, marriage
cases.held: The Court struck down Section 497 of the Indian Penal Code, which made adultery a crime only for a man who had relations with another man's wife, and treated the wife as her husband's property. The law was arbitrary and discriminatory and violated women's dignity. Adultery can still be a ground for divorce, but it is no longer a crime.

cases.name: Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala
cases.topics: Sabarimala temple, entry of women, religious practices, essential religious practice, freedom of religion
cases.held: By 4 to 1, the Court struck down the rule that kept women aged 10 to 50 out of the Sabarimala temple in Kerala, holding that excluding women for biological reasons violated their freedom of worship and equality. Justice Indu Malhotra dissented, saying courts should not interfere with essential religious practices.
cases.later: In 2019, while hearing review petitions, the Court referred wider questions on religious freedom to a larger bench; the 2018 judgment was not stayed.

cases.name: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (Aadhaar)
cases.topics: Aadhaar, biometric identity, privacy, money bill, bank accounts, mobile numbers, welfare benefits
cases.held: By 4 to 1, the Court upheld the Aadhaar Act, 2016 for welfare benefits and subsidies, and found it had been validly passed as a money bill. But it struck down Section 57, which let private companies demand Aadhaar, and held that Aadhaar cannot be made compulsory for bank accounts, mobile connections or school admissions. Justice D.Y. Chandrachud dissented.

cases.name: State (NCT of Delhi) v. Union of India
cases.topics: Delhi government, Lieutenant Governor, powers of the elected government, union territory
cases.held: The Court held that under Article 239AA the Lieutenant Governor of Delhi must generally act on the aid and advice of the elected Council of Ministers, except on public order, police and land, which belong to the Centre. The Lieutenant Governor can refer a difference of opinion to the President only in exceptional cases, not on every matter. Delhi is not a full State.
cases.later: In 2023 another Constitution Bench held that Delhi's elected government controls its civil services; Parliament then changed this by amending the law on the government of Delhi.

cases.name: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India
cases.topics: internet shutdown, Jammu and Kashmir, section 144 orders, freedom of the press, online trade
cases.held: Ruling on the communication shutdown in Jammu and Kashmir after August 2019, the Court held that freedom of speech and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the internet are protected by Article 19. Orders suspending the internet must be published, be necessary and proportionate, last only for a limited time and be open to review; repeated orders under Section 144 cannot be used to suppress legitimate expression.

cases.name: Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India
cases.topics: EWS reservation, economically weaker sections, 103rd Amendment, 10 percent quota
cases.held: By 3 to 2, the Court upheld the 103rd Amendment (2019), which allows up to 10% reservation in education and public jobs for economically weaker sections. Reservation based only on economic criteria does not violate the basic structure, and the majority upheld leaving out Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes (who have their own reservations) from this quota.

cases.name: Supriyo Chakraborty v. Union of India
cases.topics: same-sex marriage, marriage equality, queer couples, Special Marriage Act, adoption, civil unions
cases.held: The Court unanimously held that the Constitution does not give a fundamental right to marry, and that it could not rewrite the Special Marriage Act to include same-sex couples; that is for Parliament. By 3 to 2, it also declined to recognise civil unions or allow queer couples to adopt jointly. It recorded the Union government's statement that a committee would examine the practical entitlements of queer couples.

cases.name: In Re: Article 370 of the Constitution
cases.topics: Jammu and Kashmir, special status, abrogation of Article 370, statehood, Ladakh
cases.held: A five-judge bench unanimously upheld the 2019 Presidential orders that made Article 370 inoperative and applied the whole Constitution to Jammu and Kashmir. It held that Article 370 was a temporary provision and that Jammu and Kashmir had no internal sovereignty after joining India. It upheld the creation of the Union territory of Ladakh, and directed elections to the Jammu and Kashmir Assembly by 30 September 2024 and the restoration of statehood as soon as possible.

cases.name: Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (Electoral Bonds)
cases.topics: electoral bonds, political funding, donations to political parties, right to information, elections
cases.held: The Court unanimously struck down the Electoral Bond Scheme, 2018 and the related changes to election and company law, which allowed anonymous donations to political parties and unlimited donations by companies. Voters' right to information about political funding is part of freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). The State Bank of India was ordered to disclose the details of bonds bought and redeemed.
